title: Even So: con todo, aun así

sections.content:
You know *aunque* from A2 Unit 28 and *a pesar de que* from B1 Unit 32: they put a difficulty inside the sentence (*Aunque llovía, salimos*). You also know *sin embargo* from A2 Unit 28 and *no obstante* from B1 Unit 1. Two more markers say that something stays true in spite of everything just said:

• *aun así*: "even so", "all the same". It starts a new clause and points back at the whole previous statement: *Estaba cansado; aun así, salió a correr.* In speech it is the more common of the two.
• *con todo*: "even so", "for all that", a little more formal. It also points back at everything said so far.

The difference from *aunque*: *aunque* sits inside one sentence, before the difficulty. *Aun así* and *con todo* start a new clause, after a semicolon or a full stop, and name the result.

sections.title: Even so
rows: Estaba cansado; aun así, salió a correr.
He was tired; even so, he went running.
Llovía mucho; con todo, el partido continuó.
It was raining hard; even so, the match went on.
Aunque estaba cansado, salió a correr.
Although he was tired, he went running.
El camino era largo y difícil. Con todo, llegaron a tiempo.
The road was long and hard. Even so, they arrived on time.

sections.content: In *aun así*, the word *aun* means "even" and has no accent. *Aún* with an accent means "still" or "yet": *aún no ha llegado*. So write *aun así*, not *aún así*.
